name: Triton
production_evidence: vLLM uses Triton kernels for attention, quantization, and fused operations
TorchInductor generates Triton kernels as its GPU backend
TensorRT-LLM uses Triton for some fused kernels
strengths: Tile-centric abstraction: operates on blocks of data rather than individual threads, making it far more productive than CUDA C++
Python-based: no separate compilation step, kernels are JIT-compiled at runtime
Autotuning built-in: @triton.autotune decorator searches over block sizes, num_warps, num_stages
Performance on par with cuBLAS for matmul: the tutorial shows 206 TFLOPS FP16 on H100 at 4096x4096x4096
Fused operations: easy to fuse elementwise ops into matmul/attention kernels without writing separate kernels
MLIR-based backend since v2.0: better optimization pipeline than the original LLVM-based approach
Active development: Triton Conference 2026, regular releases, strong community
weaknesses: JIT compilation overhead: first call to a kernel triggers compilation (typically 0.5-5 seconds per kernel)
Autotuning can be expensive: each config is compiled and benchmarked, adding significant warmup time
Limited to NVIDIA and AMD GPUs: no CPU, TPU, or other accelerator support
Less control than CUDA C++: cannot express all low-level optimizations (e.g., manual warp-level primitives)
Debugging is harder: errors in generated PTX/SASS are harder to trace than CUDA C++ errors
Compile-time scales with kernel complexity: large fused kernels can take 10+ seconds to compile
TRITON_F32_DEFAULT environment variable can silently change precision behavior (ieee vs tf32 vs tf32x3)
notes: Triton is the most successful Python DSL for GPU kernel programming. The original paper (Tillet et al., MAPL 2019) demonstrated that a tile-based language could match cuBLAS/cuDNN performance. The key insight is that programmers specify operations on tiles (blocks of data) rather than individual threads, and the compiler handles thread-level mapping, shared memory allocation, and synchronization. The matmul tutorial shows real performance: 206 TFLOPS FP16 at 4096x4096x4096 on H100, which is competitive with cuBLAS. The autotuner is both a strength and a weakness: it finds good configurations automatically but adds significant warmup time. For inference, the JIT overhead is a real concern: a model with 50 unique kernel shapes could take 30-60 seconds to warm up. The Triton Conference 2026 (October 19, San Jose) signals continued investment. Supported on NVIDIA GPUs (CC 8.0+) and AMD GPUs (ROCm 6.2+). CPU support is under development but not production-ready.
